title: The outside passed pawn
summary: The pawn far from everything drags the enemy king away, and your king eats the pawns on the other side.
part.decoy.title: The pawn that drags the king
part.decoy.summary: Equal material, but one passed pawn far away: it becomes a decoy and your king does the rest.
part.down.title: A pawn down
part.down.summary: One pawn holds two, the other drags the king. What counts is not how many pawns, but where they are.
part.far.title: The farther, the better
part.far.summary: A passed pawn that is too close is just a pawn the king eats on the way. One file changes the result.
part.protected.title: Against the protected passed pawn
part.protected.summary: The king cannot eat a protected passed pawn. Against it, the outside passer becomes a target.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: Fischer's idea against Larsen, the rules to take home and a game to the end.
step.t_decoy: White to move. Each side has two pawns and one passed pawn: White's on a4, Black's on e5. Both kings are in the centre. Why is this winning for White, and what is the plan?
step.t_decoy.hint1: Compare the distances. The e5 pawn is close to both kings. The a4 pawn is far from everything.
step.t_decoy.hint2: If the black king goes after the a-pawn, how long is it away from e5 and g4? And what does your king do in that time?
step.decoyWhy: The a4 pawn is far from everything. When it moves, the black king has to run after it, or it queens. But the king cannot be in two places: while it goes to the a-file, my king goes to e5 and g4 and eats what was left there. The a-pawn is a decoy. It will die, but it takes the black king far away with it. That is why it is called an outside passed pawn: what matters is the distance, not the pawn.
step.d_decoy: Watch the whole plan. Notice where each king is when the a-pawn falls.
step.d_decoy.m1: a5. The pawn moves, and the black king already has to think about it.
step.d_decoy.m2: Kc5. Black goes after the pawn. If not, it queens.
step.d_decoy.m3: a6. One more step towards the edge.
step.d_decoy.m4: Kb6. The black king reaches the pawn. But look where it is: on b6, far from e5.
step.d_decoy.m5: Ke4. I let the a-pawn go and head to the other side. The e5 pawn has no defender.
step.d_decoy.m6: Kxa6. Black eats the decoy, in the corner of the board.
step.d_decoy.m7: Kxe5. A pawn for a pawn, but my king is in the centre and his is on the a-file.
step.d_decoy.m8: Kb5. The black king comes back, too late.
step.d_decoy.m11: Kxg4. My g3 pawn is left with the king beside it, and the black king is too far. That king and pawn ending is a win.
step.decoyMove: Your turn. White to move and win. Use the a-pawn as a decoy and, at the right moment, take the king to the other side.
step.decoyMove.hint: First the a-pawn moves and drags the black king. When the black king is close to it, go after the e5 pawn.
step.decoyMove.done: That's it. The black king is tied to the a-file, and your king has reached the e5 pawn. Now eat and win.
step.t_down: White to move. White is a pawn down: two against three. Even so, White wins, and with only one move. Which, and why?
step.t_down.hint1: Look at the queenside: two black pawns against one white. Can a single pawn hold both?
step.t_down.hint2: On the kingside each side has a passed pawn: yours on h3, Black's on f5. Which of the two is farther from the centre?
step.downWhy: First, b5. That pawn alone holds a7 and b6: if either of them moves, I capture and I am the one with a passed pawn. Then compare the kingside passed pawns. My h-pawn is on the edge of the board; Black's, on f5, is closer to the centre. Mine is the outside one. I will give it up to drag the black king to the h-file, eat f5 and reach the queenside first. Only b5 wins. Any other move loses.
step.d_down: Watch how the missing pawn does not matter. Count the king moves in the race to the queenside.
step.d_down.m1: b5! One pawn holds two. Black's queenside pawns are frozen.
step.d_down.m2: Kg7. The black king comes to the centre.
step.d_down.m5: h4. The h-pawn starts to move.
step.d_down.m6: Kg6. The black king has to watch the h-pawn.
step.d_down.m7: h5+! I give up the h-pawn. It is the decoy.
step.d_down.m8: Kxh5. The black king eats it, on the edge of the board.
step.d_down.m9: Kxf5. Material is equal now, and my king is in the centre. His is on the h-file.
step.d_down.m10: Kh4. Black has nothing left to do on the kingside.
step.d_down.m11: Ke6. My king runs to the queenside.
step.d_down.m12: Kg5. The black king runs too, one step behind.
step.d_down.m15: Kc6. The b6 pawn is already under attack.
step.d_down.m17: Kb7, on the way to a7.
step.d_down.m19: Kxa7. The white king reached the queenside first, and White wins. White started a pawn down.
step.downMove: White to move and win, a pawn down. First the move that holds the queenside, then the king goes to work.
step.downMove.hint: The b4 pawn can freeze both black pawns with a single step. Then the king goes after f5 and the h-pawn becomes the decoy.
step.downMove.done: Very good. The queenside is frozen, and the h-pawn will drag the black king. The rest is the race you saw.
step.t_far: White to move. Black has a passed pawn on b5, away from the other pawns. Does it drag the white king? Or does White win? Only one move does not lose.
step.t_far.hint1: Count how many moves your king needs to eat b5, and how many to get back to e4.
step.t_far.hint2: The black king will attack e4. Your king has to come back in time to defend it.
step.farWhy: Black's passed pawn is on the b-file, just one step from my king. I take it with Kxb5 in one move and come back: Kc4, Kd3, and the e4 pawn is defended. When the black king attacks g5, my e-pawn runs. The passed pawn was not far enough: it did not drag my king, it just gave me a pawn. Any other move loses.
step.farA: Now change one thing: the black pawn on a5, one file farther. To eat it my king needs two moves, Kb5 and Kxa5, and the black king uses that time to reach e4. Here White loses with any move. One extra file turns a lost pawn into an outside passed pawn that wins.
step.farMove: White to move and win. Eat Black's passed pawn and come back in time to defend e4. All three moves are the only ones.
step.farMove.hint: First, the b5 pawn. Then the king returns by the shortest path to the side of the e4 pawn, without letting the black king through.
step.farMove.done: Exactly. The king ate the pawn and came back in time. Black's passed pawn was too close to be a decoy.
step.t_prot: White to move. Black has an outside passed pawn on h5. White has a passed pawn on c5, protected by the b4 pawn. Who wins, and how?
step.t_prot.hint1: Can the black king take the c5 pawn? Can it go away from it?
step.t_prot.hint2: If the black king cannot leave the c-pawn, who is free to go and get the h-pawn?
step.protWhy: The c5 pawn is protected by b4. The black king cannot take it, and it cannot leave either, because the pawn would run. It is stuck. My king is not: it goes to get the h5 pawn. Here the outside passed pawn drags nobody; it becomes the target. One warning: do not push c6. Away from its protection the pawn falls, and Black wins.
step.d_prot: Watch the white king go for the h-pawn. Notice that the black king can do nothing against the protected pawn.
step.d_prot.m1: Kf4, on the way to the h-pawn.
step.d_prot.m2: Kd5. The black king stands next to the c-pawn, but cannot take it.
step.d_prot.m4: Kc4. Black tries something else: attacking b4, the protecting pawn.
step.d_prot.m5: Kxh5. Black's outside passed pawn is gone.
step.d_prot.m6: Kxb4. The c-pawn is alone, but now it runs.
step.d_prot.m7: c6! The black king on b4 is outside the pawn's square. And its own b5 pawn is in the way.
step.d_prot.m10: b4. Black runs too, but far behind.
step.d_prot.m11: c8, queen. The protected pawn beat the outside passed pawn.
step.protMove: White to move and win. Go get the h-pawn and, if the black king takes b4, know what to do.
step.protMove.hint: Your king goes to the kingside. The c-pawn stays where it is while b4 protects it.
step.protMove.done: Perfect. You ate the outside passed pawn, and when the black king took b4, the c-pawn ran on its own.
step.t_fischer: White to move. This is a smaller version of a famous position. Equal material, an a-pawn against two black pawns on the kingside. What is the plan?
step.t_fischer.hint1: It is the plan from the first part. The a-pawn drags the black king. Where does your king go then?
step.fischer: In 1971, in the Candidates match, Fischer reached a position like this against Larsen, with one more h-pawn on each side. Material was equal, but the a-pawn was the outside passer. Fischer centralised his king on d4, pushed the pawn to a7 and, when the black king went to b7, took his king to e6. Larsen resigned. Here, without the h-pawns, the plan is the same: a5, or the king to e4 or e3 first. The other moves, g4, Kc3, Kd3 and Kc4, only draw.
step.recap: Three rules to take home. First: in a pawn ending, look for the passed pawn that is farthest away; it is often worth more than an extra pawn. Second: use it as a decoy. Push it until the enemy king goes after it, and take your king to the other side right away. Third: check first that it is far enough and that the opponent has no protected passed pawn. Too close, it is just a pawn the king eats; against a protected passer, it becomes the target.
step.finish: Now play this position to the end. Drag the black king with the a-pawn and go eat the pawns on the other side.
ex.e11: White to move and win. The h-pawns are blocked, and your d5 pawn is passed. Where does the king go?
ex.e11.hint: The d5 pawn can be the bait. While the black king goes to take it, where does your king need to be?
ex.e11.solution: Kd4! The king still protects d5 and already points at e5, f5, g6 and h6. The black king will take the d-pawn, and in that time the white king takes h6; the h-pawn queens. Any other move loses a tempo, and Black draws. After Kc7, any king move wins; only d6+? throws the win away. Position from La-Parca-Maldita's study (chapter "Final 83").
ex.e12: Black to move and draw. White has a passed pawn on a4, far from everything. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: Before you take anything, count: can your king reach the a-pawn?
ex.e12.solution: Ke4! The king goes straight after the a-pawn. Kxe3? looks free, but after a5 the black king is outside the pawn's square and cannot catch it. After a5, Kd5! (the only move) keeps to the shortest path. The outside passer only wins when the enemy king cannot get there; here it can, and the white king on d1 is too far from the black pawns.
ex.e13: Black to move and win. White has the outside passer on a4. On the kingside you can trade pawns or go past them. What do you do?
ex.e13.hint: After a trade, the a4 pawn becomes White's outside passer. What kind of passed pawn can the white king not take?
ex.e13.solution: h4! and, after Ke2, g5! The h-pawn is passed and g5 protects it: the white king cannot take it, and the black king is free to go and get the a-pawn. hxg4? only draws: the white king takes g4, and the a4 passer ties the black king down. Some king moves also only draw, and Kf6, Kf7 or g5 straight away lose. Against the outside passer, the protected passer wins.
ex.e14: White to move and win. Position from the study "A Remote Passed Pawn" by Chessforall321. Find the right order of moves until the white king heads for the kingside.
ex.e14.hint: The c-pawn is your outside passer. The further up it is when the black king catches it, the more time your king gains.
ex.e14.solution: c4!, c5! and c6!, and only then Kxe4! The c-pawn drags the black king to c6; with the white king on e3, the e4 pawn cannot move and just waits to be taken. After Kxc6, the white king heads for the kingside (Kf5 or Ke5), takes h5 before the black king gets back, and the g-pawn wins. Kxe4? straight away only draws: Kg4!, the black king takes g3 and its h-pawn runs alongside yours. On the first four moves, only these win.
ex.e15: White to move and win. Position from the study "Ptotected and distant passed pawn" by slimshaggy. The g-pawn is your outside passer; d5 is the black passer. Beware of the natural move.
ex.e15.hint: The white king has two jobs: the d5 pawn and the a5 pawn. The g-pawn only needs to drag the black king away, at the right moment.
ex.e15.solution: Kf5! (Kh5?, protecting the pawn, loses), and after Kd6, g5! The pawn moves and the black king has to go after it. After Ke7, Ke5!, and after Kf7, Kxd5! The black king takes g5, but the white king is already on its way to a5: Kc4 (or Kc5, Kc6) and, after Kxg5, Kb5! The white king takes a5 and the a-pawn queens. Apart from Kc4, every move is the only one that wins.
ex.e08: White to move and win. The queenside pawns are blocked, and your g-pawn is the outside passer. What is the move, and what comes next?
ex.e08.hint: The g-pawn can step forward with check. Then the white king has to stand next to it.
ex.e08.solution: g6+! and, after Kg7, Kg5! The pawn advances with check and the white king protects it. The black king is tied to it, and the white king gains time to go to the queenside or escort the pawn. On both moves the alternatives only draw. Position from chessforall123's study.
key.decoy: Equal material, but White's edge pawn is far from everything. The black king has to chase it, and meanwhile the white king captures the black pawns on the other side. White wins, whoever is to move.
key.down: A pawn down, White still wins: a single white pawn holds back Black's two queenside pawns, and the h-pawn becomes the outside passer that pulls the black king away.
key.far: Black's passed pawn is too close to the white king: the king captures it and still gets back in time to defend its own pawns. White wins.
key.farA: The same position with the black pawn one file further away: now the white king needs one more move to fetch it, and that move costs White the game. Every file counts.
key.protected: The protected passer beats the outside passer: the black king cannot leave the protected white pawn, and the white king calmly goes and captures the black pawn on the other side.
key.fischerLarsen: Fischer against Larsen, 1971 Candidates: the white edge pawn drags the black king away, and the white king captures the pawns on the other side.
history: A passed pawn is a pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it or on the neighbouring files. When it is far from the others, out on the edge of the board, it becomes a decoy: the enemy king has to go and fetch it, and your king uses that time to capture the pawns on the other side. It is one of the most common weapons in pawn endings, and it often decides the game even with equal material. Nimzowitsch said the passed pawn has a lust to expand. The most famous example is from 1971: in the Candidates match in Denver, Fischer used an edge pawn as a decoy against Bent Larsen and won without ever queening; he took that match 6–0. But the outside passer has limits, and this lesson also shows when it is not enough.
practice: Now the real ending: an a-pawn against two black pawns on the kingside, equal material. Drag the black king with the a-pawn and go eat the rest. Choose the time control and go.
